translate.output: Supreme is Heaven. Heaven is accumulated qi. When it is still, it is called qi; when it moves, it is called wind. That which moves is a planet; that which does not move is a fixed star. Fixed stars have light; planets do not have light.
translate.gold: What is highest, with nothing above it, is called 天 "heaven". Heaven is accumulated air. When it is still it is called 氣 "air"; when it moves it is called 風 "wind". Those that move are planets; those that do not move are fixed stars. Fixed stars have light of their own; planets have none.
translate.error: The translation's use of 'wind' instead of 'air' for 風 subtly alters the cosmological concept being described, as 風 typically implies a more turbulent and less fundamental force than 氣.

translate.output: Practicing calligraphy by copying the 'Thousand Character Classic' is also acceptable, but one must possess perseverance. If one copies one hundred characters from a model each day without ever missing a single day, then within a few years one will surely become a master of calligraphy. Even when extremely busy, one must complete today's lesson; do not make up for yesterday's delay today, nor prepare for tomorrow's tasks ahead of time today. Never interrupt the study of books because of family matters, and never interrupt it because an examination is approaching. Even on days spent walking, one may read in the shop; even on the day of the examination, one may read while outside the venue.
translate.gold: For practising calligraphy, copying the Thousand Character Classic is fine too, but you must persevere. Copy a hundred characters from the model every day, absolutely without a break, and in a few years you will certainly have become a calligrapher. Even when you are extremely busy, you must still finish each day's lessons on that day. Do not, because of a delay yesterday, make the work up today; and do not, because you will be busy tomorrow, do the work today in advance. On no account interrupt your daily reading because there is business at home, nor interrupt it because the examinations are approaching. Even on a travelling day you can read once you reach the inn; on an examination day you can read once you come out of the hall.
translate.error: The translation renders '切勿以家中有事而間斷看書之課' as 'Never interrupt the study of books because of family matters,' which loses the nuance of the original's specific focus on interrupting the *lesson* (課) rather than general study.

translate.output: Then, does the meaning of freedom not allow it to be practiced by individuals? Answer: How can one say such a thing? Freedom of a group is the accumulation of individual freedoms. Humans cannot survive apart from groups; if a group fails to protect its own freedom, another group will invade, suppress, and seize it from outside, in which case what individual freedom remains? I am but someone with shallow learning, yet I wish to expound this through mere brief words—how can I know whether it is possible? ... Are there those in the world who love freedom? Then please do not poison freedom so as to poison the world.
translate.gold: In that case, can freedom after all not be applied to the individual? I answer: nonsense, what talk is this? Collective freedom is the sum of individual freedoms. People cannot survive on their own apart from the group. If the group does not protect its freedom, then other groups will come from outside to invade it, oppress it and plunder it, and then what will be left of the individual's freedom? For one of shallow learning like me to try to explain it in a few paltry words: how can I know that it will do? … Are there people in the world who love freedom? Let them take care not to poison freedom, and thereby poison the world.

translate.output: On the twenty-third day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of Guangxu, the Inner Cabinet received an imperial edict: For several years, officials both within and outside China have advocated studying current affairs, mostly supporting reform for self-strengthening. Recently, several imperial decrees were issued—for example, establishing a special examination, reducing redundant troops, reforming the military examination system, and setting up primary and secondary schools—all of which had been carefully deliberated multiple times and thoroughly planned, and were only now ready to be implemented. However, public opinion has not yet fully opened; opinions remain divided. Some, claiming to act out of concern for the nation and respect for experienced statesmen, argue that old regulations must be strictly followed and new methods must be completely rejected. Many voices clamor with empty words that offer no real benefit. Consider the current situation: if we still rely on untrained troops, limited funds, scholars without practical knowledge, and craftsmen without competent teachers, while strength and weakness contrast sharply and poverty and wealth are vastly unequal, how can we truly wield a simple stick to strike armored soldiers wielding sharp weapons? ... The Imperial University in Beijing serves as the model for all provinces; it should be established first. It is ordered that the Grand Councilors and the Ministers in Charge of Affairs with Foreign Countries jointly deliberate promptly and submit a proper report. ... This edict is hereby promulgated for general knowledge. So be it.
translate.gold: On the 23rd day of the 4th month of the 24th year of Guangxu, the Grand Secretariat received the following edict: For several years now, officials at court and in the provinces have studied current affairs, and most have advocated reform and self-strengthening. Recently edicts have been issued one after another: setting up a special examination, cutting surplus troops, reforming the military examinations, establishing schools of all levels. All were examined again and again and planned most thoroughly, and it has only just been proposed to put them into effect. But attitudes are not yet open, and opinions cannot agree. Some take cover behind experience and concern for the country, holding that the old institutions must be held fast and the new methods rejected. Many mouths clamour, but empty words are of no help. Let us ask: with the situation as it is today, and the state's strength as it is, if we still rely on untrained troops and limited funds, with scholars lacking practical learning and artisans lacking good teachers, the strong and the weak set side by side, the rich and the poor so far apart, can we really make clubs to beat strong armour and sharp weapons? … The Imperial University in the capital is to be an example to the provinces and above all should be set up first. Let the Grand Councillors and the princes and ministers of the Zongli Yamen deliberate on it jointly and report properly and quickly by memorial. … Let this be proclaimed to all. Respect this.
translate.error: The translation's rendering of “中外臣工” as “officials both within and outside China” is slightly misleading; it likely refers to officials in the capital and in the provinces, not foreign officials.

translate.output: The Minister of the Interior, Cheng Dequan, submits this report. It is understood that protecting the people and safeguarding the nation makes police administration a central mechanism of governance; selecting talented individuals for office requires schools as reservoirs of human resources. Nanjing, now the foremost model region, must first implement thorough improvements in all police matters to serve as an example for other provinces. However, since our department was recently established, funding is difficult; therefore, regarding donations and contributions, we should strive for strict economy. Accordingly, the former Jiangnan Higher Police Academy has been reorganized into the Ministry of the Interior's Police School. We have initially recruited 240 police trainees from the training center, organized them into specialized departments for instruction, as a temporary measure to address urgent needs. As for regular class students, once funds are secured, we will conduct new examinations and enroll them accordingly, in accordance with His Excellency the President's intention to promote public happiness. We have immediately appointed Sun Runyu, Director of Police Affairs at our Ministry, to concurrently serve as Principal of the Police School, to ensure swift implementation, thereby benefiting both public and private interests. The reasons for establishing the Police School are hereby formally submitted for review and approval. This concludes the memorial.
translate.gold: Cheng Dequan, Minister of the Interior, reports as follows. I humbly consider that for protecting the people and defending the state, police affairs are the key to administration; and for choosing the worthy and employing the able, schools are the place where talent is gathered. I note that Nanjing is now the capital, and all police matters must first be thoroughly reformed before it can serve as a model for the provinces. But this ministry has only just been founded and funds are difficult, so all measures should, it seems, be as economical as possible. I have therefore converted the existing Jiangnan Higher Police School into the Ministry of the Interior Police School. It will first recruit 240 police cadets for the training institute and teach them by subject, as an emergency measure. As for students of the regular course, as soon as definite funds have been raised, they will be admitted by examination and educated, so as to fulfil the President's intention of working to advance the people's happiness. I have also at once appointed Sun Runyu, head of this ministry's police bureau, as principal of the police school concurrently, in the hope of setting it up quickly, so that both public and private interests may benefit. As to the opening of the police school, it is proper to prepare this document and request you to examine it and put it into effect. This petition is necessary. According to your petition, the land on the west shore of Lake Shaobo has long lain waste, and you representatives cannot bear to leave its profit in the ground and plan to reclaim and cultivate it. This truly cannot be delayed. But you should measure in mu how much land there is on that shore, draw a map and first submit them to the ministry, so that we can pass them on with an order to the civil governor of Yangzhou to verify. You representatives are directed to comply at once, and also to draw up proper regulations and procedures for raising capital, and submit them to the ministry together. This is the ruling.
translate.error: The translation renders '竊維' as 'It is understood', which loses the nuance of humble self-deprecation and deference characteristic of 文言 writing; '竊' indicates a personal opinion offered with some hesitancy.

Article 1: The Treaty of Nanking, concluded on the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month in the previous Renyin year (1842), shall continue to be observed. The old Supplementary Agreement and Commercial Regulations previously established by Guangdong have now been incorporated into the new treaty; therefore, all such prior agreements are hereby declared void.

Article 50: Hereafter, all official documents from Britain shall be written in English characters only. For the time being, Chinese translations may accompany them until China has dispatched students to study English and they become proficient; at that point, Chinese translations will no longer be required. From now on, in any matter involving textual interpretation or debate, English shall serve as the authoritative standard. The current treaty was carefully compared in both Chinese and English versions without error, and this rule applies accordingly.

Article 51: Hereafter, in all official documents—whether issued from the capital or elsewhere—references to officials and citizens of Great Britain must not be written using the term 'Yi' (a derogatory word for foreigners).
translate.gold: Article 1: The peace treaty concluded earlier at Jiangning on the 24th day of the 7th month of the renyin year remains in force. The supplementary treaty concluded in Guangdong and the trade regulations are now revised; since they have been incorporated into the new treaty, all the old treaties are null and void. Article 50: From now on, British communications shall all be written in English. For the time being they will still be accompanied by Chinese; as soon as China has selected and sent students to learn English and they are proficient in the language, Chinese will no longer be sent with them. From now on, whenever there is a dispute about wording, the English shall in all cases be taken as the correct meaning. The treaty now concluded, of which the Chinese and English texts have been carefully checked and found without error, is also subject to this rule. Article 51: From now on, in official documents of all kinds, whether in the capital or the provinces, the character 夷 may not, of course, be written in referring to British officials and subjects.
translate.error: The translation incorrectly identifies the Renyin year as 1842; the Renyin year was 1842, but the treaty referred to is not the Treaty of Nanking, which was signed in 1842.

punctuate.output: 赫胥黎獨處一室之中，在英倫之南，背山而面野。檻外諸境，歷歷如在几下。乃懸想二千年前，當羅馬大將愷徹未到時，此間有何景物？故知不變一言決非天運，而悠久成物之理，轉在變動不居之中。是當前之所見，經廿年、卅年而革焉可也；更二萬年、三萬年而革亦可也。特據前事推將來，為變方長，未知所極而已。雖然，天運變矣，而有不變者行乎其中。不變惟何？是名天演。以天演為體，而其用有二：曰物競、曰天擇。此萬物莫不然而於有生之類為尤著。物競者，物爭自存也。以一物以與物，物爭或存或亡，而其效則歸於天擇。天擇者，物爭焉而獨存，則其存也必有其所以存；必其所得於天之分，自致一己之能，與其所遭值之時與地，及凡周身以外之物力，有其相謀相劑者焉。夫而後獨免於亡，而足以自立也。而自其效觀之，若是物特為天之所厚而擇焉以存也者，夫是之謂天擇。天擇者，擇於自然；雖擇而莫之擇，猶物競之無所爭而實天下之至爭也。斯賓塞爾曰：「天擇者，存其最宜者也。」夫物既爭存矣，而天又從其爭之後而擇之。一爭一擇，而變化之事出矣。

translate.output: Huxley, alone in a room in southern England, with his back to the mountains and facing the wilds, could see clearly from outside the lattice all the scenes around him. He then imagined what the landscape was like two thousand years ago, before the Roman general Caecilius had arrived... Thus we know that the statement 'nothing changes' is certainly not true of the course of nature. The principle by which things come into being over long periods lies instead in constant change. What is seen before us may be transformed after twenty or thirty years; it may also be transformed after two or three ten thousand years. We can only infer from past events that change continues indefinitely, without knowing its ultimate limit. Nevertheless, while the course of nature changes, there are elements within it that do not change. What remains unchanged? This is called 'natural evolution.' Taking natural evolution as the substance, its function has two aspects: competition among things and selection by nature. All living things follow this pattern, especially those capable of life. 'Competition' means things striving to preserve themselves. One thing competes with other things; some survive, others perish, and the result is determined by natural selection. 'Selection by nature' means that among competing things, only some survive. For such survival to occur, there must be reasons: it must possess what nature has allotted to it, its own inherent abilities, the time and place it encounters, and all external forces surrounding it; these factors must work together in a coordinated and balanced way. Only then can it avoid extinction and establish itself independently. From the perspective of its effect, such a thing is specially favored by nature and thus selected to survive—this is what we call 'selection by nature.' Selection by nature operates according to natural laws: though it selects, nothing actively chooses; just as competition appears without struggle, it is in fact the utmost form of struggle. Herbert Spencer said: 'Selection by nature preserves that which is most suitable.' Since things already compete for survival, and nature follows this competition to select among them, one act of competition followed by one act of selection gives rise to change.
translate.gold: Huxley is sitting alone in a room in the south of England, with hills behind and fields in front; the scenes beyond the railing are as clear as if they lay below his desk. He then imagines what this place looked like two thousand years ago, before the Roman general Caesar came. …… Hence we know that "unchanging" is by no means the way of heaven's course, and that the principle by which things endure and take shape lies, on the contrary, in ceaseless change. What we see before us may well be transformed in twenty or thirty years, or again in twenty or thirty thousand. It is only that, inferring the future from past events, change has far still to run, and we do not know where it will end. And yet, though heaven's course changes, something unchanging operates within it. What is this unchanging thing? It is called evolution (天演). Evolution is the substance, and it has two functions: the struggle of things (物競) and the selection of heaven (天擇). This is so of all things, and most evident among living things. The struggle of things is things striving to preserve themselves. When one thing contends with thing after thing, it either survives or perishes, and the result comes down to the selection of heaven. The selection of heaven is when things contend and one alone survives. Then there must be a reason for its survival: its endowment from heaven, the abilities it attains by itself, the time and place it meets with, and all the forces of things outside its body must have worked together and complemented one another. Only then does it alone escape perishing and become able to stand on its own. And looking at it from the result, it is as if this thing had been specially favoured by heaven and selected to survive: this is what is called the selection of heaven. The selection of heaven is selection by nature: it selects, yet no one selects; just as the struggle of things seems to be no struggle, and is in truth the fiercest struggle in the world. Spencer said: "The selection of heaven is the preservation of the fittest." Since things struggle to survive, and heaven then selects among them after their struggle, with each struggle and each selection, change comes about.
translate.error: The translation renders '愷徹' as 'Caecilius,' which is an incorrect transliteration of the Roman general Cneius Caesar; the reference translation correctly identifies him as Caesar.

punctuate.output: 中國政治與文化之變革，莫劇於殷周之際。殷周間之大變革，自其表言之，不過一姓一家之興亡與都邑之移轉；自其裏言之，則舊制度廢而新制度興，舊文化廢而新文化興。又自其表言之，則古聖人之所以取天下及所以守之者，若無以異於後世之帝王；而自其裏言之，則其制度文物與其立制之本意，乃出於萬世治安之大計，其心術與規摹，迥非後世帝王所能夢見也。欲觀周之所以定天下，必自其制度始矣。周人制度之大異於商者：一曰立子立嫡之制，由是而生宗法及喪服之制，並由是而有封建子弟之制、君天子臣諸侯之制；二曰廟數之制；三曰同姓不婚之制。此數者皆周之所以綱紀天下，其旨則在納上下於道德，而合天子、諸侯、卿大夫、士、庶民以成一道德之團體。周公制作之本意實在於此。此非穿鑿附會之言也。茲篇所論皆有事實爲之根據，試略述之。其條例則《春秋左氏傳》之說曰：「太子死，有母弟則立之；無則立長。年鈞擇賢，義鈞則卜。」公羊家之說曰：「禮嫡夫人無子，立右媵；右媵無子，立左媵。」此二說中，後說尤爲詳密。顧皆後儒充類之說，當立法之初，未必窮其變至此。然所謂「立子以貴不以長，立適以長不以賢」者，乃傳子法之精髓；當時雖未必有此語，固已用此意矣。

translate.output: The transformation of Chinese politics and culture was no more profound than between the Yin and Zhou dynasties. ... From an external perspective, the great transformation between Yin and Zhou was merely the rise and fall of one family and the relocation of the capital; from an internal perspective, old systems were abolished and new ones established, old culture discarded and new culture adopted. Again, from an external view, the ancient sages' methods for acquiring and maintaining the world seemed no different from later emperors; but from an internal view, their institutions, cultural artifacts, and the original intent behind establishing them were designed for universal peace and order, with moral principles and planning far beyond what later emperors could even imagine. To understand how Zhou stabilized the world, one must begin with its institutions. The major differences between Zhou systems and Shang are: first, the system of establishing sons as heirs based on legitimacy (the principle of primogeniture), from which arose the clan system and mourning attire regulations, and also the feudal system for appointing brothers and the structure of emperor over vassal lords; second, the system of ancestral temple counts; third, the prohibition against marriage within the same surname. These three elements formed the framework by which Zhou governed the world. Their purpose was to integrate upper and lower strata into morality, uniting the emperor, vassal lords, ministers, officials, and common people into a single moral community. The original intent behind Duke of Zhou's institutional creations lies precisely here. This is not forced or fanciful interpretation; the arguments in this essay are all grounded in historical facts, which I will briefly outline. ... Regarding the rules, the Spring and Autumn Annals (as interpreted by Zuo Qiuming) states: 'If the crown prince dies, appoint his younger full brother; if none exists, appoint the eldest son. If ages are equal, choose the more capable one; if moral standing is equal, resort to divination.' The School of Gongyang offers another view: 'According to ritual, if the primary consort bears no son, establish the right concubine (the first secondary wife); if she also bears no son, establish the left concubine (the second secondary wife), ...' Between these two accounts, the latter is more detailed, yet both are later scholars' extrapolations. At the time when laws were originally formulated, such elaborate variations may not have been fully anticipated. However, the core principle of 'establishing heirs based on status rather than age, and selecting legitimate successors based on seniority rather than virtue'—though these exact words may not have existed then—their underlying meaning was already in practice.'
translate.gold: Of all the changes in China's government and culture, none is more drastic than that at the transition from Shang to Zhou. …… The great change between Shang and Zhou, seen from the surface, was no more than the rise and fall of one family and the moving of the capital; seen from within, old institutions fell and new institutions arose, old culture fell and new culture arose. Again, seen from the surface, the ways in which the ancient sages won the empire and kept it seem no different from those of later emperors; but seen from within, their institutions, their culture and their original intention in founding the institutions came in fact from a grand plan for order and peace for ten thousand generations, and their thinking and design were far beyond anything later emperors could dream of. If one wishes to see how the Zhou settled the empire, one must begin from its institutions. The Zhou institutions that differ greatly from the Shang are, first, the institution of succession by the son and by the son of the principal wife, from which arose the lineage system and the mourning system, and from which came the enfeoffment of sons and younger brothers and the system in which the Son of Heaven is lord and the feudal lords are subjects; second, the number of ancestral temples; third, the rule that those of the same surname do not marry. These are all the means by which the Zhou gave order to the empire. Their purpose was to bring high and low within morality, and to unite the Son of Heaven, the feudal lords, ministers, great officers, gentlemen and the common people into one moral community. The Duke of Zhou's original intention in making institutions truly lay here. These are not far-fetched or forced words: everything this essay argues has facts as its evidence. Let me set it out briefly. …… The rules are given in the account of the *Zuo Commentary*: "When the heir dies, if there is a younger brother by the same mother, he is made heir; if not, the eldest is made heir. If they are equal in age, the worthiest is chosen; if equal in merit, the matter is divined." The Gongyang school's account says: "By the rites, if the principal wife has no son, the son of the right secondary wife is made heir; if the right secondary wife has no son, the son of the left secondary wife is made heir; ……" Of these two accounts, the latter is especially detailed, but both are the extrapolations of later Confucians; when the rule was first laid down, its makers did not necessarily work out every case in this way. Yet what is called "a son is made heir by rank, not by age; the son of the principal wife is made heir by age, not by worth" is the essence of the rule of succession by sons; though these words may not have been said at the time, the idea was certainly already in use.

translate.output: My younger brother has long been a friend of Mr. Jifang, and through him I have heard of Yuanfang's excellence; I have always wished to meet him for my own satisfaction. Yesterday, while in Huicheng, I happened to encounter him, and found that your elder brother's talent and bearing are even greater than what I had heard. I truly regret meeting him so late; unexpectedly, after just one night we parted ways, and now I regret the speed of our separation. After parting, on the fourth day I arrived in Tianjin, and on the tenth day I visited Pingshu. In less than a month, I have traveled through two places. Tired from dust and wind, I am merely working as a clerk, which makes me pity myself and even laugh at myself. Now that my fellow officials are returning to their hometowns, I am the only one left in the office; moreover, with the clear bell and red fish, it feels exactly like practicing cultivation in an ancient temple. Yet, as the west wind blows and yellow leaves fall, memories of our past times often arise; surely the two carp will not abandon me. Is your health fully restored? With wedding affairs causing much trouble, please take good care of yourself. Sending this by way of the wind to convey my thoughts; there is much more I wish to express but cannot say here. For a long time I have not seen the graceful appearance of green wutong and bamboo; whenever the moon is bright and the wind is clear, I deeply long for them. Furthermore, I have been suspicious that you have not recently served in the capital. Recently I received a letter from Mr. Ruan Xihou, learning that your carriage has traveled to the left of the mountains, and that planting lotus at Chuqiu has already been going on for more than one day. Green reeds and jade-green stones are sold everywhere; this is naturally so. Your younger brother's talent and spirit, I fully believed would be like a solitary crane on Jishan, sufficient to lift the spirits of the chicken flock; who expected that the zither was broken and the grass on the grave had already settled overnight, causing deep sighs! My younger brother first stayed as a guest in western Liaoning, then traveled to Tianjin. This spring again there was the matter of Pingshu. Year after year I am pressed by deadlines, still working as a hired hand; this is truly because village women with beautiful eyebrows are hard for the times to appreciate.
translate.gold: I, your younger brother, formerly had the good fortune to make friends with your younger brother, and so heard of your worth as the elder, and longed for the pleasure of meeting you. Yesterday I met you by chance in the provincial capital, and felt that your talent and bearing surpassed even what I had heard. Just as I was regretting that we had not met sooner, we unexpectedly parted after a single night, and now I regret that we were separated so soon. After we parted, I reached Tianjin on the fourth and went to Pingshu on the tenth: in less than a month I have changed place twice. Travel-worn, I do nothing but weed other people's fields; I pity myself, and can also laugh at myself. Just now my colleagues have gone home, and I live alone in the office; add the clear chime and the red wooden fish, and it is just like an old temple for religious practice. With the west wind and the yellow leaves, I often long for you deeply; you will surely not abandon me, but will send me a letter. Have you recovered your health? With the wedding arrangements so many and tiring, please take good care of yourself. I send my thoughts by the wind, and cannot express all I feel. I have long not seen your bearing, like green parasol trees and jade bamboo; whenever the moon is bright and the wind clear, I long for you in spirit. I had wondered why you had not been on duty for so long. Recently I received a letter from Ruan Xihou and learnt that you have travelled to Shandong and have long been serving in a secretariat at Chuqiu. Fine swords and fine jade are sought after everywhere: that is only to be expected. Your younger brother's talent and spirit, I was sure, like Ji Shao, the lone crane, would shine among the flock of chickens. Who could have expected that Boya's zither would be broken, and that the grass on the grave is already a year old? It moves one to sorrow! I, your younger brother, first lived in Liaoxi, then soon moved to Tianjin and its lakes. This spring I have again taken up a post at Pingshu. Year after year I sew for others, still a hired hand: truly because a village girl's fine eyebrows are hard for the age to admire.
translate.error: The translation renders '碧梧翠竹' as 'green wutong and bamboo,' which loses the specific, evocative imagery of the original; wutong and bamboo are not the same as the original plants.
